topic_lead: Against fate and fixed natures, the early fathers insist that human beings can choose — or the language of reward, blame, counsel, and judgment collapses. Voices range from the well-known apologists to Methodius, Hermas, and Lactantius.
author: Justin Martyr
english: But so that no one, from what we said earlier, will think we claim that events happen by the necessity of fate — just because they were foretold as things known in advance — we will clear this up too.
We have learned through the prophets, and we declare it true, that punishments, chastisements, and good repayments are given according to the worth of each person’s deeds.

If that were not so, and everything instead happened by fate, then nothing at all would be in our power. For if it is fated that this one be good and that one worthless, then the first is not to be approved and the second not to be blamed.
And again: unless the human race has power, by free deliberate choice, to flee what is shameful and to choose what is fine, it is not accountable for whatever is done.

But that it both succeeds and fails by free deliberate choice, we prove as follows. We see the same human being turning to pursue opposite things. If it had been fated that he be either worthless or excellent, he would never have been able to receive both opposites, nor change so often.

Nor would some be excellent and others worthless — for then we would make fate the cause of both good and worthless things, acting against itself — or else that earlier claim would seem true: that there is no virtue and no vice, only opinion labeling things good or bad, which, as the true Word shows, is the greatest impiety and injustice.
But we say this is unbreakable ‘fate’: that those who choose what is fine receive fitting rewards, and those who likewise choose the opposite receive fitting wages.

For God did not make the human being like other things — trees and four-footed animals — that can do nothing by choice. He would not deserve reward or praise if he did not choose the good from himself, but were simply made that way; nor, if he were bad, would he justly meet with punishment, not being such from himself, but unable to be anything other than what he had been made.
translator_notes: Source-locked to First1KGreek Justin 1 Apology 43. See justification receipt for προαίρεσις ἐλευθέρα and fate vocabulary.

note_anchors.note: Grk προαίρεσις ἐλευθέρα (“free deliberate choice”). Or “free choice.”
Grk εἱμαρμένην…ἀπαράβατον; Justin’s ironic redefinition of “fate” as the fixed outcome of choice.

author: Justin Martyr
english: Among us the prince of the wicked demons is called the serpent and Satan and the devil, as you can learn by looking into our writings. Christ foretold that he would be sent into the fire with his host and the people who follow him, to be punished without end.

For God delays the fulfillment of this because of the human race: he foreknows that some will be saved by repentance, and some even that have not yet been born. In the beginning he made the race with the power to choose the truth and do good; so that all people are without excuse before God, for they were born able to reason and reflect.

author: Justin Martyr
english: As many as are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and who undertake to be able to live accordingly, are taught to pray and ask God with fasting for the forgiveness of their past sins, while we pray and fast with them.

Then they are brought by us to where there is water, and in the manner of regeneration by which we ourselves were regenerated they are regenerated. For in the name of God the Father and Master of all, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they then wash in the water.
translator_notes: Baptism tied to persuaded faith and a willing new way of life — not bare coercion.

added_allusions.reason: New birth / water.

author: Barnabas
english: See how he set the water and the cross together. For this is what he means: blessed are those who hoped in the cross and went down into the water. This means that we go down into the water loaded with sins and dirt, and we come up bearing fruit in the heart — the fear and the hope that are toward Jesus, held in the Spirit.

author: Tatian
english: Evil does not have the nature of the good — that nature belongs to God alone. Among human beings it is completed by the freedom of deliberate choice, so that the worthless person is justly punished, having become wicked through himself, and the just person is worthily praised for noble deeds, not having transgressed God's will by the self-determining power given from God.
translator_notes: Source-locked Tatian Oratio ad Graecos Greek. Replaces shorter ANF-mediated draft.

note_anchors.note: Grk ἐλευθερία τῆς προαιρέσεως. Or “freedom of choice.”

author: Athenagoras
english: As with human beings, who have virtue and vice by their own choice (αὐθαίρετον) — for you would neither honor the good nor punish the wicked if vice and virtue were not in their power, and some prove faithful in what you entrust to them while others prove unfaithful — so it is also with the angels.

Some, free to choose as God made them, stayed in what God made and ordered them to be. Others abused both the substance of their being and their rule: the ruler over matter and its forms, and others among those around the first firmament.
translator_notes: Philosophical Athenian tone — keep the cool precision.

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: If he turns instead to the works of death, disobeying God, he himself is the cause of his own death. For God made the human being free and self-determining.
What he procured for himself through carelessness and disobedience, God now gives him through his own kindness and mercy — when the human being obeys him.
Just as by disobeying, the human being drew death on himself, so by obeying the will of God, the one who wants to can procure eternal life for himself. For God gave us a law and holy commandments.
translator_notes: Source-locked Theophilus Ad Autolycum Greek (First1K/Perseus).

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: And this too was a great kindness God provided for the human being: that he should not remain forever in sin. In a kind of exile he cast him out of paradise, so that by the chastisement he might pay the debt of sin in due time, and after being disciplined might later be recalled.

That is why, when the human was formed in this world, Genesis mysteriously writes of him as placed twice in paradise: the first placement already fulfilled when he was set there, and the second still to be fulfilled after the resurrection and judgment.

And just as a vessel, once formed, if it takes on some fault, is remelted or refashioned so that it may become new and whole, so it is with the human through death: he has in effect been shattered so that in the resurrection he may be found sound — spotless, just, and immortal.
As for God’s calling out, “Where are you, Adam?” — he was not doing this as one who did not know, but, being long-suffering, he was giving Adam an opening for repentance and confession.

Τὸ δὲ καλέσαι καὶ εἰπεῖν τὸν θεόν· «Ποῦ εἶ, Ἀδάμ;» οὐχ ὡς ἀγνοῶν τοῦτο ἐποίει ὁ θεός, ἀλλὰ μακρόθυμος ὢν ἀφορμὴν ἐδίδου αὐτῷ μετανοίας καὶ ἐξομολογήσεως.

author: Irenaeus
english: That saying — “How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were not willing” — set out the ancient law of human liberty. From the beginning God made man free, possessing his own power, just as he possesses his own soul, so that he might use God’s counsel voluntarily and not as one forced by God.

Force does not come from God; good counsel is always with him. For that reason he gives good counsel to all. He also placed in man the power of choice, as also in the angels — for angels too are rational — so that those who obeyed might justly possess the good: given by God, kept by themselves.
translator_notes: Pastoral-polemical weight; keep Scripture woven in.
Continuous Against Heresies witness is Latin; Greek fragmentary — not pretended as Greek source.

added_allusions.reason: How often I wanted… you would not.

author: Irenaeus
english: If it were not in our power to do these things or not to do them, what point would there be in counsel from the apostle — and much more from the Lord himself — to do some things and abstain from others?

But because man has been of free decision from the beginning, and God — whose likeness he bears — is of free decision, counsel is always given him to hold to the good, which is completed in obedience to God. And not only in works but also in faith has the Lord preserved man’s free decision and his power under his own control, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you,” showing that a person’s faith is his own, because he has his own judgment.

Again: “All things are possible to the one who believes,” and, “Go; as you have believed, be it done to you.” All such things show that man is under his own power according to faith. On this account the one who believes has eternal life, and the one who does not believe the Son does not have eternal life, but the wrath of God remains on him.

On this reasoning, showing his own good and marking man as of his own decision and under his own power, the Lord said to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not! Therefore your house is left to you desolate.”
translator_notes: Glossary: liberum…suae potestatis arbitrium / liberae sententiae → free decision / under his own control — not bare “free will.”

latin: Si igitur non in nobis esset facere haec, aut non facere, quam causam habebat Apostolus, et multo prius ipse Dominus, consilium dare, quaedam quidem facere, a quibusdam vero abstinere? Et non tantum in operibus, sed etiam in fide, liberum et suae potestatis arbitrium hominis servavit Dominus, dicens: Secundum fidem tuam fiat tibi; propriam fidem hominis ostendens, quoniam propriam suam habet sententiam. Quapropter relinquetur vobis domus vestra deserta.

author: Irenaeus
english: Offer him your heart soft and workable, and keep the form in which the Craftsman shaped you, keeping moisture in yourself so that you do not harden and lose the marks of his fingers.

Keeping the jointing, you will rise to the perfect. Soft clay is hidden in you by God’s craft. He will overlay you inside and out with pure gold and silver, and adorn you until the King himself desires your beauty.

But if you harden at once and spit out his art and prove thankless that you were made human, you lose both his art and life. To make belongs to God’s kindness; to be made belongs to human nature. Hand him what is yours — faith in him and subjection — and you will receive his art and be a perfect work of God.
translator_notes: Cooperation image: willing clay, not coerced stone — preserve the metaphor.

note_anchors.note: Irenaeus’s image: the clay must stay soft under the Craftsman’s hand.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Among the Greek philosophers, human self-control claims to fight desire and not to serve it in deeds. Among us it is not to desire at all — not that someone who desires should merely tough it out, but that he should be continent even of desiring. And this self-control cannot be received in any other way than by the grace of God. That is why he said, “Ask, and it will be given you.”

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: What is voluntary is either by appetite, or by deliberate choice (προαίρεσις), or by thought. Sin, mishap, and injustice sit next to one another in this range: living in luxury and license is a sin; striking a friend as an enemy from ignorance is a mishap; tomb-robbery or temple-robbery is injustice.

Sinning comes from not knowing what must be done, or from being unable to do it. But it is in our power (ἐφ’ ἡμῖν) both to present ourselves for training and to obey the commandments. If we refuse to share in them, we will sin — or rather, wrong our own soul.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We were not called children and infants for a childish, contemptible lesson. Regenerated, we have at once received the perfect — which is why we were hurrying. For we were illuminated; and that means to know God. The one who knows the perfect is not incomplete.

To believe only and to be regenerated is perfection in life; God is never weak. As his will is work and that work is called world, so his wish is the salvation of human beings, and that is called church. The one newly regenerated — as the name shows — being illuminated, is at once freed from darkness and receives the light.

author: Tertullian
english: I find that man was set up by God free — of his own decision and of his own power. I notice no greater image and likeness of God in him than this form of status.

For he was not stamped toward the one God by face and bodily lines — so varied in the human race — but in that substance he drew from God himself, that is the soul, marked toward God’s form, which pledges the freedom and power of his own decision.

The law God then set confirmed this status. A law would not be laid on someone who did not have the owed obedience to the law in his own power; nor would the threat of death be written against transgression if contempt of the law were not charged to man as freedom of decision.
So also in the later laws of the Creator you will find him setting before man good and evil, life and death.

So full freedom of decision was granted him toward either side, that as his own master he might steadily meet good by keeping it willingly and evil by avoiding it willingly — since a man set under God’s judgment had to make that judgment just by the deserts of his own free decision. Otherwise neither reward for good nor for evil could rightly be weighed out to someone who turned out good or evil by necessity, not by willing.

author: Tertullian
english: If people shared in God — and so also in reason — they would first weigh what repentance is worth, and would never use it to enlarge a crooked “improvement.” They would temper the measure of repenting because they would also hold the measure of sinning — fearing the Lord.

But where there is no fear, there is likewise no amendment; where there is no amendment, repentance is necessarily empty, because it lacks its fruit — the fruit for which God sowed it, that is, human salvation.

After so many and such great sins of human rashness, beginning from Adam the head of the race — after man was condemned with the world’s dowry, cast out of paradise and subjected to death — when God again ripened toward his mercy, he dedicated repentance in himself first: he revoked the sentence of earlier wrath and covenanted to forgive his own work and image.
translator_notes: si dei ac per hoc rationis quoque compotes: “shared in God — and so also in reason,” not bare “had God’s reason.”

author: Hippolytus
english: The human being who was made was a self-determining living creature (αὐτεξούσιον) — not a ruling mind holding all things by thought and power, but a servant, with opposites present in him. Because he is self-determining, he generates evil, which comes about as an accident: it is nothing unless you do it. Evil is named in the willing and thinking of something bad; it was not from the beginning, but comes on later.

Because he is self-determining, a law was set by God — not in vain. If man did not have the power to will and not to will, why was a law set at all? Law is not laid down for an irrational animal — bit and whip are — but for a human being: command and penalty for doing what is ordered and for not doing it.

author: Origen
english: Since the church’s proclamation includes the word about God’s just judgment — and those who trust it are called to live well and flee sin in every way, agreeing that what deserves praise or blame is in our power — let us also treat briefly of self-determination (τὸ αὐτεξούσιον), a most necessary question.

Of things that move, some have the cause of motion in themselves; others are moved only from outside. Wood and stones are moved only from outside. Animals and plants have the cause in themselves. Rational living beings also have reason, which judges the impressions, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the creature may be led by them. We choose the fine and turn from the shameful — and are praiseworthy or blameworthy accordingly. What falls on us from outside is not in our power; judging how to use what has happened is the work of the reason in us.

author: Origen
english: Toward the saying “it is not of the one who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy,” Solomon’s ascent-psalm helps: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.”

This does not stop us from building or watching. It shows that what is built without God, and what lacks his guard, is built in vain and kept without result. If we say this building is God’s work, not the builder’s, we are not wrong — something has happened on the human side, yet the successful deed is thankfully referred to God who brings it to completion. Human willing is not enough for the end, nor is the athletes’ running enough to take the prize.

author: Origen
english: Celsus thinks it impossible that those divided across Asia, Europe, and Libya — Greeks and barbarians to the ends — should ever agree in one law, and says that whoever thinks so knows nothing.

We say it is not only possible but true that the whole rational nature will one day come under the Word and be remade into his perfection — when each, using bare power of choice (ἐξουσία), chooses what he wills and comes to be in what he chose.

It is not likely that, as some bodily wounds outrun every medical art, so some evils of the soul should be impossible for the Logos and God over all to heal. The Word is stronger than every evil in the soul; his therapy comes to each by God’s will, and the end of things is the removal of evil.
translator_notes: Compressed paraphrase of Origen’s anti-determinist apologetic line; expand on Greek pass.

author: Anonymous (Diognetus)
english: For God loved human beings — the ones for whom he made the world, to whom he subjected everything on the earth, to whom he gave reason and mind, whom alone he allowed to look upward toward him, whom he formed from his own image, to whom he sent his only-begotten Son, to whom he promised the kingdom in heaven — and he will give it to those who have loved him.

author: Methodius of Olympus
english: Orthodox: I do not think it right to say that human beings were made by God as mere necessities. I say the first human was made self-determining — that is, free — and from him the heirs of the race inherited the same freedom.

So I affirm that the human being was made free, yet a slave to whatever he wills to serve. I say this is the greatest gift given him by God. For all other things serve the divine command by necessity: if you speak of heaven, it stands bearing its Master, not leaving its appointed place; if of the sun, it completes its set course, not refusing the run, but serving the Master by a kind of necessity.

Earth likewise you see fixed and bearing the command of the one who ordered it. The rest also serve the Maker by necessity, none of them able to do anything other than that for which it was made. Therefore we do not praise them for obeying the Master this way, nor is a better hope laid up for them, because they kept the command unwillingly.

But the human being received authority to obey whatever he wills, bringing himself into service — not mastered by necessity of nature, nor stripped of power. I say this was granted for the sake of better things, so that he might receive something more than he has from the Better One — something that comes to him from obedience and that he may claim from his Maker as what is due.
translator_notes: Source-locked Methodius De Libero Arbitrio (First1KGreek). Dialogue speaker: Orthodox.

The same rule of truth teaches us to believe, after the Father, also in the Son of God, Christ Jesus, our Lord and God — but the Son of God, that is, of that God who is both one and alone, the maker of all things.

author: Lactantius
english: Someone will say: why then does God allow these things to happen and not rescue people from such bad errors? So that evils may fight with goods, so that vices may stand against virtues, so that he may have some to punish and others to honor.

For in the last times he has appointed to judge the living and the dead — of which judgment I will speak in the last book. So he delays until the end of times comes, when he will pour out his wrath in heavenly power and might, as the predictions of the pious prophets terrify with a dreadful warning.

For now he allows people to err and even to be impious against him — he himself being just and mild and patient. It cannot be that the one in whom there is perfect virtue should not also have perfect patience.

author: Arnobius
english: Does Christ not free all with equal munificence? Does he not free equally when he calls all equally? He opens the fountain of life to all; no one is forbidden to drink.

If you scorn the gift, why does the one who invites wait? His only part is to set the fruit of his kindness under the decision of your own right (sub tui iuris arbitrio). Plato said the lot of choosing a life is not God’s doing as a cause forced on another; free decision (voluntatis libertas) sits in the power of the one who willed.
God lays necessity on no one; he terrifies no one with bullying fear. Our salvation is not so necessary to him that he gains or loses something if he makes us gods or lets us dissolve into nothing.
translator_notes: Obscure to most Logos users; sharp pagan-world apologetic.

author: Arnobius
english: Since this is so, what injustice is so great that we seem fools to you for believing these things, when we see you both believing similar things and living in the same expectation? If we are thought worthy of mockery because we promise ourselves a hope of this kind, the same mockery awaits you who claim for yourselves a hope of immortality. If on other grounds you hold and follow reason, grant us also some share of that reason.

If Plato in the Phaedrus — or someone else from that company — had promised us these joys, that is, a way of escaping death, and could furnish it and bring the promises to their end, it would have been fitting for us to take up cults of the one from whom we would await so great a gift and favor.

As it is, since Christ has not only promised it but has also shown by such great powers that it can be fulfilled, what strange thing are we doing, or by what reasons do we bear the charge of folly, if we bow to his name and majesty — from whom both the expectation of so great a gift awaits us, and, in things already past, hope of things still to come has been conceived?

author: Minucius Felix
english: Let no one take comfort from fate or excuse what happens by it. Let there be a lot of fortune — the mind is still free; and so a person’s acts, not status, are judged.

What else is fate but what God has spoken (fatus) concerning each of us? Since he can foreknow the material, he also sets the fates according to each one’s deserts and qualities. So it is not birth-chart that is punished in us, but the nature of the character.

author: Minucius Felix
english: Do you think we hide what we worship because we have no shrines and altars? What image should I fashion for God, when — if you judge rightly — the human being is himself God’s image? What temple should I raise for him, when this whole world, made by his work, cannot contain him? And when I, a human, am more spacious still, should I shut the force of such majesty inside one little chapel? Is he not better dedicated in our mind, consecrated in our inmost heart?

Should I offer God victims and sacrifices that he brought forth for my use, so as to throw his own gift back at him? That is thankless, when the acceptable victim is a good spirit, a pure mind, and a sincere judgment. So the one who cultivates innocence prays to God; the one who cultivates justice pours him a libation; the one who keeps from fraud propitiates God; the one who snatches a human from danger slays the best victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God’s sacred rites: among us the more just person is the more religious.

But, you say, the God we worship we neither display nor see. On the contrary: we believe God precisely because we can perceive him and cannot see him. In his works and in all the motions of the world we always behold his power present — when it thunders, flashes, strikes, when the sky clears. Do not wonder that you do not see God: wind and blasts drive, shake, and agitate all things, yet wind and blast do not come under the eyes.

But, you say, God does not know human action, and set in heaven he cannot either go about to all or know each one. You err, O human, and are deceived. How is God far off, when all things heavenly and earthly — and what lies beyond this province of the world — are full of God? Everywhere he is not only nearest to us, but poured into us.
translator_notes: Underfilled Latin author; new locus beyond Octavius 36 fate/judgment slice.
True worship: human as image, pure mind as victim, God unseen yet near/infusus.

author: Commodian
english: Our first preface shows the way to the one who wanders, and the good regard that comes when the world’s turning-point arrives — to become eternal, which ignorant hearts refuse to believe.

I myself wandered a long time the same way, chasing shrines, my parents not knowing better. Reading the Law finally pulled me out. I testify to the Lord: I grieve for the civic crowd that goes on perishing, seeking empty gods. So, taught at last, I instruct the ignorant in the truth.

author: Hermas
english: First of all, believe that God is one — who created and framed all things, who brought all things from non-being into being, who contains all things and alone is uncontained.

Trust him, then, and fear him; and having feared him, practice self-control. Keep these things, and you will throw all wickedness off yourself, put on every virtue of righteousness, and live to God — if you keep this commandment.
translator_notes: Popular in antiquity, sidelined in modern reading lists — include.

author: Hermas
english: You say: “Lord, these commandments are great and fine and glorious, and they can gladden the heart of anyone who can keep them. But I do not know whether a human being can keep them, because they are very hard.” He answered: “If you set it before yourself that they can be kept, you will keep them easily and they will not be hard. But if it already rises in your heart that a human being cannot keep them, you will not keep them.”

Those who have the Lord on their lips, but whose heart is hardened and far from the Lord — for them these commandments are hard and difficult to walk. So you who are empty and light in the faith: put your Lord into your heart, and you will know that nothing is easier than these commandments — or sweeter, or gentler.

author: Barnabas
english: There are two ways of teaching and of authority: the way of light and the way of darkness. And the difference between the two ways is great. Over the one stand light-bearing angels of God; over the other, angels of Satan. The one is Lord from ages to ages; the other is the ruler of the present age of lawlessness.

english: If Jesus Christ counts me worthy through your prayers, and if it is his will, I will explain to you more carefully in a second booklet what I have begun about the plan that leads to the new man, Jesus Christ.

It concerns his faith and his love, his suffering and resurrection — especially if the Lord shows me that you all gather man by man in grace, in one faith and in Jesus Christ, who is of David’s line according to the flesh, Son of man and Son of God, so that you obey the bishop and the presbytery with an undivided mind, breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying, so that we may live in Jesus Christ forever.

author: Ignatius of Antioch

author: Mathetes (Epistle to Diognetus)
english: When our unrighteousness was fulfilled, and it was fully shown that its wages — punishment and death — were to be expected, then the time came which God had appointed to show his kindness and power.

He did not hate us or reject us or remember evil. He was patient. In mercy he took up our sins. He gave his own Son as a ransom for us — the holy for the lawless, the innocent for the wicked, the just for the unjust, the incorruptible for the corruptible, the immortal for the mortal.

citation: Dionysius of Alexandria — On Nature (via Eusebius PE 14.23–24)
author: Dionysius of Alexandria
english: Some give the name “atoms” to certain imperishable and most minute bodies, infinite in number, and they put forward a void of unbounded extent. These atoms, they say, are borne about at random in the void, collide of themselves through an irregular rush, and tangle because they are many-shaped and catch hold of one another — and so produce the world and what is in it, or rather worlds without number. Epicurus and Democritus held this view.

How are we to bear with them when they say that the wise and therefore beautiful works of creation are chance coincidences? Works of which each, as it came into being by itself, and likewise all of them together, were seen to be good by the One who commanded them to be made. For Scripture says: “And God saw all things that he had made, and behold, they were very good.”

They are not even instructed by the small, familiar examples at their feet, from which they could learn that no useful work made for benefit is finished without design or by mere accident, but is crafted by hand for its fitting service — and only when it falls into uselessness is it dissolved and scattered at random, because the wisdom that cared for its standing no longer manages or orders it.

greek: οἶ μὲν γὰρ ἀτόμους προσειπόντες ἄφθαρτά τινα καὶ σμικρότατα σώματα πλῆθος ἀνάριθμα, καί τι χωρίον κενὸν μέγεθος ἀπεριόριστον προβαλόμενοι, ταύτας δή φασι τὰς ἀτόμους ὡς ἔτυχεν ἐν τῷ κενῷ φερομένας αὐτομάτως τε συμπιπτούσας ἀλλήλαις διὰ ῥύμην ἄτακτον καὶ συμπλεκομένας διὰ τὸ πολυσχήμονας οὔσας ἀλλήλων ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι, καὶ οὕτω τόν τε κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ κόσμους ἀπείρους ἀποτελεῖν. ταύτης δὲ τῆς δόξης ’Επίκουρος γεγόνασι καὶ Δημόκριτος· τοσοῦτον δὲ δὲ διεφώνησαν ὅσον ὁ μὲν ἐλαχίστας πάσας καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀνεπαισθήτους, ὁ δὲ καὶ μεγίστας εἶναί τινας ἀτόμους ὁ Δημόκριτος ὑπέλαβεν. ἀτόμους δὲ εἶναί φασιν ἀμφότεροι καὶ λέγεσθαι διὰ τὴν ἄλυτον στερρότητα. οἶ δὲ τὰς ἀτόμους μετονομάσαντες ἀμερῆ φασιν εἶναι σώματα, τοῦ παντὸς μέρη, ἐξ ὧν ἀδιαιρέτων ὄντων συντίθεται τὰ πάντα καὶ εἰς ἃ διαλύεται. καὶ τούτων φασὶ τῶν ἀμερῶν ὀνοματοποιὸν Διόδωρον γεγονέναι· ὄνομα δὲ, φασὶν, αὐτοῖς ἄλλο Ἡρακλείδης θέμενος ἐκάλεσεν ὄγκους, παρ’ οὗ καὶ Ἀσκληπιάδης ὁ ἰατρὸς ἐκληρονόμησε τὸ ὄνομα.” Ταῦτ’ εἰπὼν ἐξῆς ἀνασκευάζει τὸ δόγμα διὰ πολλῶν, ἀτὰρ καὶ διὰ τούτων ‟Πῶς αὐτῶν ἀνασχώμεθα τυχηρὰ λεγόντων εἶναι συμπτώματα τὰ σοφὰ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὰ καλὰ δημιουργήματα; ὣν ἕκαστόν τε καθ’ ἑαυτὸ γενόμενον ὤφθη τῷ προστάξαντι γενέσθαι καλὸν καὶ συλλήβδην ὁμοίως ἅπαντα. καὶ εἶδε γὰρ, φησὶν, ὁ θεὸς τὰ πάντα ὅσα ἐποίησε, καὶ ἰδοὺ καλὰ λίαν. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ ἀπὸ τῶν μικρῶν τῶν συνήθων καὶ παρὰ πόδας νουθετοῦνται παραδειγμάτων, ἐξ ὧν δύνανται μανθάνειν ὅτι χρειῶδες μὲν καὶ πρὸς ὠφέλειαν ἔργον οὐδὲν ἀνεπιτηδεύτως οὐδὲ συμβατικῶς ἀπεργάζεται, ἀλλὰ χειρουργούμενον εἰς τὴν πρέπουσαν ὑπηρεσίαν καταρτίζεται· ὅταν δὲ εἰς ἄχρηστον μεταπίπτῃ καὶ ἀνωφελὲς, τότε διαλυόμενον ἀορίστως καὶ ὡς ἂν τύχῃ διασκίδναται, ἅτε μηκέτι μεταχειριζομένης μηδὲ διαταττούσης αὐτὸ τῆς σοφίας, ᾗ τοῦ συνεστάναι τοῦτο ἔμελεν.

author: Tatian
english: But we ourselves stand above fate. Instead of wandering demons we have learned one Master who does not wander, and since we are not driven by fate we have refused the ones who wrote its laws.

author: Victorinus of Pettau
work: On the Creation of the World
english: On the fifth day land and water brought forth their young. On the sixth day the things still lacking were created; and so God formed the human being from the soil as lord of all he had made on land and water. Yet he created angels and archangels before he fashioned the human, putting spiritual things before earthly ones. For light was before heaven and earth. This sixth day is called parasceve — preparation of the kingdom. He completed Adam after his image and likeness. For that reason he finished his works before he created the angels and fashioned the human, lest they falsely claim they had been his helpers.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: This is the one after the image and likeness: the true knower, who imitates God as far as he can, leaving out nothing that belongs to that possible likeness — self-controlled, enduring, living justly, ruling his passions, sharing what he has as he is able, and doing good in word and deed. He is greatest in the kingdom, Scripture says, who both does and teaches, imitating God by giving gifts of the same kind. For God’s gifts are for the common good.
greek: Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ κατ’ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν, ὁ γνωστικός, ὁ μιμούμενος τὸν θεὸν καθ’ ὅσον οἷόν τε, μηδὲν παραλιπὼν τῶν εἰς τὴν ἐνδεχομένην ὁμοίωσιν, ἐγκρατευόμενος, ὑπομένων, δικαίως βιούς, βασιλεύων τῶν παθῶν, μεταδιδοὺς ὧν ἔχει, ὡς οἷός τέ ἐστιν, εὐεργετῶν καὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ. οὗτος μέγιστος, φησίν, ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ ὃς ἂν ποιῇ καὶ διδάσκῃ μιμούμενος τὸν θεὸν τῷ παραπλήσια χαρίζεσθαι· κοινωφελεῖς γὰρ αἱ τοῦ θεοῦ δωρεαί.

author: Irenaeus
english: God gave the good, as the apostle also testifies in the same letter. Those who work it will receive glory and honor, because they worked the good when they were also able not to work it.

Those who do not work it will receive God’s just judgment, because they did not work the good when they were able to work it. The showing is not that some are good by nature and others evil, but that the good lies in human choice.

author: Justin Martyr
english: We do not say that what happens to people is done or suffered by fate. Each person succeeds or sins by deliberate choice (προαίρεσις), and wicked demons also work against the serious — as they did against Socrates and his like — while a Sardanapalus or an Epicurus seems to prosper.

The Stoics missed this and declared that everything happens by fate’s necessity. But God made both the race of angels and of human beings self-determining (αὐτεξούσιον) from the beginning; therefore they justly receive punishment in eternal fire for whatever they do wrong.
It is the nature of everything that has come to be to be capable of vice and virtue. Nothing of theirs would be praiseworthy if it did not also have the power to turn either way.

author: Tatian
english: How then am I to accept a birth under fate, when I see such “managers” of it? I do not want to be king. I do not want to be rich. I have refused generalship. I have hated fornication. I do not sail for greed. I do not compete for crowns. I am free of glory-madness. I despise death. I rise above every kind of sickness. Grief does not consume my soul.

If I am a slave, I endure slavery; if I am free, I do not boast of noble birth. I see one sun for all, and one death for all through pleasure and lack. We were not made in order to die — we die through ourselves. Self-determining power (τὸ αὐτεξούσιον) ruined us; we who were free became slaves; we were sold through sin. God made nothing base; we displayed the wickedness — and those who displayed it are also able to refuse it again.

author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: The tree of knowledge was not evil as a tree; disobedience was evil. Knowledge itself is good when used rightly. Adam was still a child; he could not yet receive knowledge as he should.
That is why God forbade him to take from the tree for a time — not from jealousy, but so that he might grow first. Disobedience finally brought death.
translator_notes: Removed earlier “obedience would have brought life” clause — that parallel sits in Ad Autolycum 2.27, not in the locked 2.25 Greek block.

author: Clement of Alexandria
english: I know many who continually attack us and say that what does not hinder is a cause. They say the one who did not guard, or did not prevent, is cause of a theft — as the one who did not put out a fire at the start is cause of the blaze, and the pilot who did not furl the sail is cause of shipwreck. The law even punishes such “causes.”

We answer that a cause is understood in doing and acting and effecting, while what does not hinder is, as such, inactive. The cause stands with the activity — as the shipbuilder with the ship’s coming to be.
translator_notes: Stromata 1.17 is providence/causation (μὴ κωλῦον ≠ αἴτιον), not the ANF “drag by the hair” locus.

author: Lactantius
english: This is why someone who would rather go without or die than harm another or snatch something seems foolish — people think a human being is destroyed by death. From that persuasion come the errors of the crowd and of the philosophers.

If after death we are nothing, it is most foolish not to manage this life so that it lasts long and is full of every advantage — and whoever does that must leave the rule of justice. But if a better and longer life remains for a human being — which we learn from great philosophers’ arguments, oracles of seers, and divine voices of prophets — then it is the wise person’s part to despise the present with its goods, since every loss is weighed against immortality.

author: Methodius of Olympus
english: How then do you say he left the qualities of the worthless as they were? Was he able to remove them too, but unwilling — or did he lack the power?

If you say he was able but unwilling, you must call him their cause: able to make them not be bad, he allowed them to remain as they were — especially when he began to craft the matter. If he had no care for matter at all, he would not be cause of what he let remain; but since he crafts one part and leaves another as it is, though able to turn that too toward the better, he seems to me to incur blame for leaving a wicked part of matter to the ruin of what he crafted.

author: Mathetes (Epistle to Diognetus)
english: Christians are not distinguished from the rest of people by land, language, or customs. They live in Greek and barbarian cities as each one’s lot falls; they follow local customs in dress and food and the rest of life.

Yet they show a striking and admittedly paradoxical citizenship of their own. They live in their own countries — but as sojourners. They share all things as citizens, and endure all things as foreigners. Every foreign land is a homeland to them, and every homeland a foreign land.

If you do not have living water, baptize in other water; if you cannot use cold, use warm.
If you have neither, pour water on the head three times in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Before the baptism let the baptizer and the one being baptized fast, and any others who can. You are to tell the one being baptized to fast for one or two days beforehand.

He said these things to the Son. I will show you again how he speaks to us: he made a second formation in the last times.

author: Hermas
english: “Hear now,” he said, “about faith. There are two angels with a human being: one of righteousness and one of wickedness.”
“How then, Lord,” I said, “will I know their workings, since both angels live with me?”

“Hear,” he said, “and you will understand them. The angel of righteousness is tender, shamefast, gentle, and quiet. You are beaten, senseless one: the God who founded the world lives, whose lawful claims cry out that they still hold for the dead. While you rush to live without God, you judge a person extinguished in the fates, or you believe it is fate. The eternal God did not arrange it as you think — that the dead are forgetful of what they did before. He has now made for us the holding-places of death for the unskilled; but after our ashes we will see those things. Tear yourself free, fool, who think that after the funeral you are not. You have made out that your Ruler and Lord can do nothing. But death is not into a void, if you turn it over in the heart. Know what should be hoped for — for late you will feel him.

You were ruler of the flesh; certainly the flesh was not ruling you. Freed from it, that flesh of yours is stored away. Rightly is a mortal human separated from flesh. Therefore mortal eyes will not be able to match this — so deep is our abyss concerning God’s secrets. So now, while you are fragile and dying, give honor to God, and believe that Christ makes you alive again from the dead. You ought to return praises to the Almighty in the church.

author: Lactantius
english: Let people learn and understand why the highest God, when he was sending his legate and messenger to instruct mortality with the precepts of justice, willed him to be clothed with flesh and afflicted with torment and punished by death. For since there was no justice on earth, he sent a teacher as a living law, to found a new name and temple, to sow true and pious worship through the whole earth by words and by example.

Yet so that it would be certain he was sent by God, he did not need to be born as a human is born, compounded from both mortal parents; but so that it would appear that even in the human he was heavenly, he was created without a father’s agency. For he had God as the spiritual father — and as the father of his spirit is God without a mother, so the mother of his body is a virgin without a father.

He was therefore both God and human, set as middle between God and human — which is why the Greeks call him mediator — so that he might be able to lead the human to God, that is, to immortality. Because if he had been God only, as said above, he could not offer humans examples of virtue; if human only, he could not compel humans toward justice unless authority and power greater than a human were added.

author: Lactantius
english: I have spoken about humility and frailty and suffering — why God preferred to undergo these. Now the reason of the cross itself must be given and its force told. What the highest Father disposed from the beginning, and how he ordered all things that were done, is taught not only by the prophets’ foretelling, which truly went ahead into Christ, but also by the reason of the passion itself. For whatever he suffered was not empty, but had a great figure and meaning — just as those divine works he did also did: their force and power were effective for the present, yet they also declared something for the future.

He was — that is, innocent and just and holy — who, sacrificed by those same Jews, is for salvation to all who have written on their own forehead the sign of the blood, that is, of the cross by which he poured out blood. For the forehead is the human’s highest threshold, and wood smeared with blood is a signification of the cross. Finally the immolation of the animal by those who keep the Passover is named from “to suffer,” because it is a figure of the passion, which God, foreknowing things to come, handed over through Moses for his people to celebrate. But then the figure prevailed in the present toward driving away danger, so that it might appear how much the truth itself would prevail toward protecting God’s people in the extreme necessity of the whole world.

author: Lactantius
english: First, then, people ought to know that the highest God’s plan proceeded from the beginning this way: as the end of the age drew near, it was necessary for God’s Son to descend to earth in order to constitute a temple for God and teach justice — yet not in an angel’s virtue or heavenly power, but in human form and mortal condition; and when he had finished his teaching office, he would be handed over into the hands of the impious and take up death, so that death too, subdued by virtue, might rise again, and so that to the human whom he had put on and was bearing he might both offer hope of conquering death and admit him to the rewards of immortality.

Lest anyone not know this plan, we will teach that all things we see completed in Christ were foretold. Let no one lend faith to our assertion unless I show that the prophets, long beforehand, foretold that God’s Son would someday be born as a human, do wonders, sow the worship of God through the whole earth, and finally be fixed to the gibbet and rise again on the third day. When I have proven all this from the very writings of those who violated their God while he used a mortal body, what else will stand in the way of it being clear that true wisdom dwells in this religion alone?

author: Lactantius
english: Perhaps someone may ask how, when we say we worship one God, we nevertheless assert that there are two, God the Father and God the Son. This assertion drives many into the greatest error. Though what we say seems probable to them, they think we waver in this one point—that we confess both another God and a mortal God. We have already spoken about mortality; now let us teach about unity. When we say God the Father and God the Son, we do not say something different, nor do we separate the two, because neither can the Father be separated from the Son nor the Son from the Father, if indeed the Father cannot be named without the Son nor can the Son be generated without the Father. When therefore the Father makes a son and the Son a father, there is one mind for both, one spirit, one substance: but the former is like an overflowing fountain, the latter like a stream flowing down from him; the former like the sun, the latter like a ray stretched from the sun. And since he is both faithful and dear to the highest Father, he is not separated, just as neither stream from fountain nor ray from sun, because both the fountain’s water is in the stream and the sun’s light is in the ray; equally neither voice can be severed from the mouth nor virtue or hand torn away from the body.

Wherefore, when the mind and will of the one is in the other—or rather one in both—rightly either is called one God, because whatever is in the Father flows across to the Son and whatever is in the Son descends from the Father. Therefore that highest and singular God cannot be worshiped except through the Son. Whoever thinks he worships the Father alone, just as he does not worship the Son, so he does not even worship the Father. But whoever receives the Son and bears his name—that one truly worships the Father together with the Son, since the Son is legate and messenger and priest of the highest Father. This one is the door of the greatest temple, this the way of light, this the leader of salvation, this the doorway of life.

author: Lactantius
english: From these things it appears that all the prophets announced concerning Christ that at some time, born bodily from David’s line, he would establish an eternal temple for God—which is called the church—and call all nations together to the true religion of God. This is the faithful house, this the immortal temple, in which if anyone has not sacrificed, he will not have the reward of immortality. And since Christ was the fabricator of a temple both great and eternal, the same one must also have in it an everlasting priesthood, nor can one arrive at the temple and at the sight of God except through him who established it. David teaches that very thing in Psalm 109, saying: “Before the daystar I begot you. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest forever.”

And who he would be to whom God was promising an eternal priesthood, Zechariah also taught most openly with the name set down. He, however, exhibited faithfulness to God: for he taught that there is one God and that he alone must be worshiped, and he never said that he himself was God, because he would not have kept faith if, sent to remove gods and assert one, he introduced another besides the one. For this reason—because he stood out so faithful, because he took nothing at all for himself, that he might fulfill the sender’s commands—he received both the dignity of perpetual priest and the honor of highest king and the power of judge and the name of God.

author: Lactantius
english: When Christ was fulfilling what God had willed and had foretold through his prophets many ages earlier, those who did not know the divine writings gathered to condemn their God. Knowing this would happen, and saying again and again that he must suffer and be killed for the salvation of many, he withdrew with his disciples—not to escape what he had to endure, but to show that in every persecution one must not seem to have fallen by his own fault—and he announced that he would be betrayed by one of them. They offered him to Pontius Pilate and demanded that he be fixed to a cross, charging him with nothing except that he said he was the Son of God and king of the Jews, and that he had said: “If you destroy this temple, which was built in forty-six years, I will raise it in three days without hands,” signifying his coming passion and that, killed by the Jews, he would rise on the third day. For he himself had been the true temple of God. Pilate found nothing worthy of condemnation in him, yet under the crowd’s shouts and Herod’s pressure he handed him over; they flogged him, mocked him as king with a scarlet robe and thorns, gave him gall and vinegar, spat on him, cast lots for his clothes, and hung him between two robbers—while he uttered no word, as if mute.

What shall we say of the unworthiness of this cross, on which God was hung and fixed by the worshipers of God? The prophets and the Sibylline songs had already announced that these things would happen. Moses said a hanging life would be before their eyes; Zechariah: “They will look upon me whom they pierced”; David in Psalm 21: they dug his hands and feet, numbered his bones, divided his garments and cast lots for his clothing—not of himself as king, but of the one the Spirit spoke of, who would suffer those things ages later. Solomon also prophesied that Jerusalem would perish in vengeance for the holy cross: they abandoned the Lord their God, persecuted their king most beloved to God, and crucified him in great humility—and for this God brought these evils upon them.

uictus est, nec tamen ipse sententiam protulit, sed tradidit eum Iudaeis, ut ipsi de illo secundum legem suam iudicarent. duxerunt igitur eum flagellis uerberatum et priusquam cruci adfigerent, inluserunt: indutum enim coloris punicei ueste ac spinis coronatum quasi regem salutarunt et dederunt ei cibum fellis et miscuerunt ei aceti potionem. post haec conspuerunt faciem eius et palmis ceciderunt. cumque ipsi carnifices de uestimentis eius contenderent, sortiti sunt inter se de tunica et pallio. et cum haec omnia fierent, nullam uocem ex ore suo, tamquam si mutus esset, emisit. tum suspenderunt eum inter duos noxios medium, qui ob latrocinia damnati erant, crucique fixerunt. quid ego hic in tanto facinore deplorem aut quibus uerbis tantum nefas conquerar? non enim Gauianam crucem describimus, quam Marcus Tullius uniuersis eloquentiae suae neruis ac uiribus uelut effusis totius ingenii fontibus prosecutus est, facinus indignum esse proclamans ciuem Romanum contra omnes leges in crucem esse sublatum. qui quamuis innocens fuerit et illo supplicio indignus, mortalis tamen et ab homine scelesto qui iustitiam ignoraret adfectus. quid de huius crucis indignitate dicemus, in qua deus a cultonbus dei suspensus est atque subfixus? quis tam facundus et tanta rerum uerborumque copia instructus existet, quae oratio tantae affluentiae ubertate decurrens, ut illam crucem merito deploret, quam mundus ipse et tota mundi elementa luxerunt? haec autem sic futura esse et prophetarum uocibus et Sibyllinis carminibus denuntiatum est. aput Esaiam ita scriptum inuenitur: non sum contumax neque contradico: dorsum meum posui ad flagella et maxillas meas ad palmas, faciem autem meam non auerti a foeditate sputorum. similiter Dauid in psalmo XXXIIII: congregata sunt in me flagella et ignorauerunt, dissoluti sunt nec conpuncti sunt: temptauerunt me et deriserunt derisum, striderunt super me dentibus suis. Sibylla quoque eadem futura monstrauit: εἰς ἀνόμους χεῖρας καὶ ἀπίστων ὕστερον ἥξει, δώσουσι δὲ θεῷ ῥαπίσματα χερσὶν ἀνάγνοις, καὶ στόμασιν μιαροῖσι ἐμπτύσματα φαρμακόεντα· δώσει δ᾽ εἰς μάστιγας ἁπλῶς ἁγνὸν τότε νῶτον. item de silentio eius, quod usque ad mortem pertinaciter tenuit, Esaias iterum sic locutus est: sicut ouis ad immolandum adductus est et sicut agnus coram tondentibus sine uoce, sic non aperuit os suum. et Sibylla supra dicta: καὶ κολαφιζόμενος σιγήσει, μή τις ἐπιγνῶ τίς λόγος ἢ πόθεν ἦλθεν, ἵνα φθιμένοισι λαλήσει, καὶ στέφανον φορέσει τὴν ἀκάνθινον.

de cibo uero et potu, quem antequam figerent ei obtulerunt, Dauid in psalmo LXVIII sic ait: et dederunt in escam meam fel et in siti mea potum mihi dederunt acetum. idem hoc futurum etiam Sibylla contionata est: εἰς δὲ τὸ βρῶμα χολὴν καὶ εἰς δίψαν ὄξος ἔδωκαν, τῆς ἀφιλοξενίης ταύτην δείξουσι τράπεζαν. Et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat increpat: et alia Sibylla Iudaeam terram his increpat uersibus: αὐτὴ γὰρ δύσφρων, τὸν σὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἐνόησας παίζοντα θνητοῖσι νοήμασιν, ἀλλὰ ἀπ\' ἀκάνθης ἔστεψας στεφάνῳ φοβερὴν τε χολὴν ἐκέρασσας. fore autem ut Iudaei manus inferrent deo suo eumque interficerent, testimonia prophetarum haec antecesserunt. aput Hesdram ita scriptum est: et dixit Hesdras ad populum: hoc pascha saluator noster est et refugium nostrum. cogitate et ascendat in cor uestrum, quoniam habemus humiliare eum in signo: et post haec sperabimus in eum, ne deseratur hic locus in aeternum tempus, dicit dominus deus uirtutum. si non credideritis ei neque exaudieritis adnuntia tionem eius, eritis derisio in gentibus. unde apparet Iudaeos nullam aliam spem habere nisi se abluerint a sanguine ac sperauerint in eum ipsum quem necauerunt. Esaias quoque facinus eorum designat et dicit: in humilitate iudicium eius sublatam est. natiuitatem eius quis enarrabit? quoniam auferetur a terra uita eius, a facinoribus populi mei abductus est ad mortem. et dabo malos pro sepultura eius et diuites pro morte eius, quia facinus non fecit neque insidias ore suo locutus est. propterea ipse consequetur multos et fortium diuidet spolia, propterea quod traditus est ad mortem et inter facinerosos deputatus est: et ipse peccata multorum pertulit et propter facinora illorum traditus est. Dauid quoque in psalmo XCIII: captabunt in animam iusti et sanguinem innocentem condemnabunt, et factus est mihi dominus in refugium. item Hieremias: domine, significa mihi, et cognoscam. tunc uidi meditationes eorum: ego sicut agnus sine malitia perductus sum ad uictimam: in me cogitauerunt cogitationem dicentes: uenite, mittamus lignum in panem eius et eradamus a terra uitam eius et nomen eius non erit in memoria amplius. lignum autem crucem significat et panem corpus eius, quia ipse est cibus ac uita omnium qui credunt in carnem quam portauit et in crucem qua pependit. de qua tamen apertius ipse Moyses in Deuteronomio ita praedicauit: et erit pendens uita tua ante oculos tuos, et timebis die ac nocte et non credes uitae tuae, idem rursus in Numeris: non quasi homo dominus suspenditur neque quasi filius hominis minas patitur. Zacharias etiam sic tradidit: et intuebuntur in me, quem transfixerunt. item Dauid in psalmo XXI: effoderunt manus meas et pedes meos, di-numerauerunt omnia ossa mea: ipsi autem contemplati sunt et uiderunt me et diuiserunt uestimenta mea sibi et super uestem meam sortem miserunt. quae utique propheta non de se locutus est. fuit enim rex et numquam illa perpessus est, sed spiritus dei per eum loquebatur, qui fuerat illa passurus post annos mille et quinquaginta, tot enim colliguntur anni a regno Dauid usque ad crucem Christi. sed et Solomon filius eius, qui Hierosolymam condidit, eam ipsam perituram esse in ultionem sanctae crucis prophetauit: quodsi auertimini a me, dicit dominus, et non custodieritis ueritatem meam, reiciam Israhel a terra quam dedi illis, et domum hanc quam aedificaui illis in nomine meo, proiciam illam es omnibus, et erit Israhel in perditionem et in inproperium populo, et domus haec erit deserta, et omnis qui transiet per illam admirabitur et dicet: propter quam rem deus fecit terrae huic et huic domui haec mala? et dicent: quia reliquerunt dominum deum suum et persecuti sunt regem suum dilectissimum deo et cruciauerunt illum in humilitate magna: propter hoc inportauit illis deus mala haec.

author: Lactantius
english: When the highest God and Parent of all had willed to transfer his religion, he sent from heaven a teacher of justice, that in him or through him he might give a new law to new worshipers—not as he had done before through a human, yet he still willed him to be born as a human, that through all things he might stand like the highest Father. For God the Father himself, origin and beginning of things, since he has no parents, is most truly named by Trismegistus fatherless and motherless, because he was begotten of no one. For that reason the Son also had to be born twice, that he himself might become fatherless and motherless: in the first, spiritual nativity he was motherless, because without a mother’s office he was generated from God the Father alone; in the second, fleshly nativity he was fatherless, because without a father’s office he was brought forth from a virgin’s womb—so that, bearing a middle substance between God and human, he might be able to lead out this fragile and weak nature of ours as by the hand unto immortality. He was made Son of God through the Spirit and of a human through the flesh, that is both God and human. The power of God in him appeared from the works he did; the frailty of the human from the passion he endured—and why he took that up I will teach a little later.

Meanwhile we learn from the prophets’ oracles that he was both God and human, mixed from both kinds. Isaiah testifies he was God: “Egypt has grown weary… for in you is God, and there is no other god besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel the Savior.” Jeremiah: “This is our God, and another will not be reckoned besides him… After this he was seen on the earth and lived with humans.” David in the psalm: “Your throne, O God, is unto ages of ages… therefore God, your God, has anointed you”—which word also shows the name, since from anointing he is called Christ. And that the same one was human Jeremiah teaches: “And he is a human, and who has known him?” Isaiah: “And the Lord will send them a human who will save them.” Moses in Numbers: “A star will rise from Jacob and a human will arise from Israel.”

Therefore both David and the other prophets announced that Christ would be generated according to the flesh from this very house. In Isaiah: “And there will be in that day the root of Jesse… in him the nations will hope.” And Nathan to David: “I will raise up your seed after you… He will build me a house in my name, and I will raise his throne unto the age, and I will be to him for a father and he will be to me for a son.” The Jews referred this to Solomon, who built a hand-made temple; but Solomon’s rule was not perpetual, he was never called Son of God, and the house he built did not obtain faith as the church does—which is the true temple of God, not in walls but in the heart and faith of humans who believe in him and are called faithful. That Solomonic temple, because it was made by hand, fell by hand.

latin: Summus igitur deus ac parens omnium cum religionem suam transferre uoluisset, doctorem iustitiae misit e caelo, ut nouis cultoribus nouam legem in eo uel per eum daret, non sicut ante fecerat per hominem, sed tamen nasci eum uoluit tamquam hominem, ut per omnia summo patri similis existeret. ipse enim pater deus, origo et principium rerum, quo-niam parentibus caret, ὰπάπωρ atque ὰμήτωρ a Trismegisto uerissime nominatur, quod ei nullo sit procreatus. idcirco etiam filium bis nasci oportuit, ut et ipse fieret ὰπάτωρ atque ὰμήτωρ. in prima enim natiuitate spiritali ὰμήτωρ fuit, quia sine officio matris a solo deo patre generatus est, in secunda uero carnali ὰπάτωρ fuit, quoniam sine patris officio uirginali utero procreatus est, ut mediam inter deum hominemque substantiam gerens nostram hanc fragilem inbecillamque naturam quasi manu ad inmortalitatem posset educere. factus est et dei filius per spiritum et hominis per carnem, id est et deus et homo. dei uirtus in eo ex operibus quae fecit apparuit, fragilitas hominis ex passione quam pertulit: quam cur susceperit paulo post docebo. interim et deum fuisse et hominem ex utroque genere permixtum prophetis uaticinantibus discimus. Esaias deum fuisse testatur his uerbis: fatigata est Aegyptus, et negotiatio Aethiopum et Sabain uiri alti ad te transgredientur et tui erunt serui et post te ambulabunt uincti conpedibus et adorabunt te et in te precabuntur: quoniam in te deus est, et non est deus alius praeter te. tu enim es deus, et nos nesciebamus, deus Israhel saluator. confundentur et reuerebuntur omnes qui aduersantur tibi, et cadent in confessionem. item propheta Hieremias sic ait: hic deus noster est et non deputabitur alius absque illo, qui inuenit omnem uiam prudentiae et dedit eam Iacob puero suo et Israhel dilecto sibi. post haec in terris uisus est et cum hominibus conuersatus est. item Dauid in psalmo XLEQI: thronus tuus, deus, in saecula saeculorum, uirga aequitatis uirga regni tui. dilexisti iustitiam, odio habuisti iniustitiam. propterea unxit te dominus deus tuus oleum exultationis. quo uerbo etiam nomen ostendit, siquidem, ut supra docui, ab unctione appellatus est Christus. deinde hominem fuisse eundem Hieremias docet dicens: et homo est et quis cognouit eum? item Esaias: et mittet eis dominus hominem, qui saluabit eos et iudicans sanabit eos. sed et Moyses in Numeris ita loquitur: orietur stella ex Iacob et exsurget homo ex Israhel. propterea Milesius Apollo consultus utrumne deus an homo fuerit, hoc modo respondit: θνητὸς ἔην κατὰ σάρκα σοϕὸς τερατώδεσιν ἕργοις, ἀλλ\' ύπὸ Χαλδαίοισι διϰασπολίαισιν ἀλώσας, γομϕωθεὶς σκολόπεσσι πιϰρὴν ἀνέπλησε τελευτήν. primo uersu uerum quidem dixit, sed argute consultorem fefellit sacramentum ueritatis penitus nescientem: uidetur enim negasse illum deum. sed cum fatetur secundum carnem fuisse mortalem, quod etiam nos praedicamus, consequens est ut secundum spiritum deus fuerit, quod nos adfirmamus. quid enim fuerat necesse carnis facere mentionem, cum satis esset dicere fuisse mortalem? sed ueritate pressus negare non potuit quemadmodum se res haberet, sicut illut, quod ait sapientem fuisse. quid ad hoc, o Apollo, respondes? si sapiens fuit, ergo doctrina eius sapientia est nec ulla alia, et sapientes qui secuntur nec ulli alii.

cur igitur uulgo pro stultis et uanis et ineptis habemur, qui sectamur magistrum etiam ipsorum deorum confessione sapientem? nam quod ait portentifica illum opera fecisse, quo maxime diuinitatis fidem meruit, adsentiri nobis iam uidetur, cum dicit eadem quibus nos gloriamur. sed colligit se tamen et ad daemoniacas fraudes redit. cum enim uerum necessitate dixisset, iam deorum ac sui proditor uidebatur, nisi quod ab eo ueritas expresserat, mendacio fallente (obs)curasset. ait ergo illum fecisse quidem opera miranda, uerum non diuina uirtute, sed magica. quid mirum, si hoc Apollo ueritatem ignorantibus persuasit, cum Iudaei quoque, cultores ut uidebantur summi dei, hoc idem putauerint, cum ante oculos eorum cottidie fierent illa miracula? nec tamen tantarum uirtutum contemplatione inpelli potuerunt ut deum crederent, quem uidebant. propterea Dauid, quem praeter ceteros prophetas uel maxime legunt, in psalmo XXVII sic eos damnat: redde illis retributionem eorum, quoniam non intellexerunt in operibus domini. ex huius ipsius domo Christum generatuiri secundum carnem et ipse Dauid et alii prophetae adnuntiauerunt. aput Esaiam ita scriptum est: et erit in illa die radix Iesse et qui exsurget principari in nationes: in eum gentes sperabunt et erit requies eius in honore. et alio loco: exiet uirga de radice Iesse et flos de radice ascendet: et requiescet super eum spiritus dei, spiritus sapientiae et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, spiritus scientiae et pietatis: inplebit illum spiritus timoris dei. Ie-ssp autem fuit pater Dauid, ex cuius radice ascensurum esse florem praelocutus est, eum scilicet, de quo Sibylla dicit ἀνθήσει δ\' ἄνθος καθαρόν. item in Basilion libro secundo propheta Nathan missus est ad Dauid uolentem deo templum fabricare. et fuit uerbum domini ad Nathan dicens: uade et dic seruo meo Dauid: haec dicit dominus deus omnipotens: non tu aedificabis mihi domum ad inhabitandum, sed cum inpleti fuerint dies tui et dormieris cum patribus tuis, suscitabo semen tuum post te et parabo regnum eius. hic aedificabit mihi domum in nomine meo et erigam thronum eius usque in saeculum, et ego ero ei in patre et ipse erit mihi in filio. et fidem consequetur domus eius, et regnum eius usque in saeculum. sed haec ut Iudaei non intellegerent, illa fuit causa, quod Solomon filius Dauid templum deo aedificauit et ciuitatem, quam de suo nomine Hierosolymam nuncupauit. itaque ad ipsum quae a propheta dicta sunt rettulerunt. Solomon autem ab ipso patre suo imperii regimen accepit. prophetae uero de eo loquebantur qui tum nasceretur, postquam Dauid cum patribus suis requieuisset. praeterea Solomonis imperium perpetuum non fuit: annis enim quadraginta regnauit. deinde, quod numquam filius dei dictus est, sed filius Dauid, et domus quam aedificauit non est fidem consecuta sicut ecclesia, quae est uerum templum dei, quod non in parietibus est, sed in corde ac fide hominum qui credunt in eum ac uocantur fideles: illut uero Solomonium templum quia manu factum est, manu cecidit. denique pater eius in psalmo CXXVI de operibus filii sui prophetauit hoc modo: si dominus non aedificauerit domum, in uanum laborauerunt qui illam aedificauerunt: si dominus non custodierit ciuitatem, in uacuum uigilauit qui eam custodiuit.

author: Lactantius
english: Descending therefore from heaven, that holy Spirit of God chose a holy virgin into whose womb he would enter. And she, filled after drinking in the divine Spirit, conceived, and without any touch of a man the virgin womb suddenly swelled. And if it is known to all that certain animals are accustomed to conceive by wind and breeze, why does anyone think it strange when we say a virgin was made heavy by the Spirit of God, to whom whatever he wills is easy? This could indeed seem unbelievable, unless the prophets had sung that it would be so many ages beforehand. Solomon in the nineteenth Ode says the virgin’s womb was weakened and received a fetus. Likewise Isaiah: “For this reason God himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin will receive in the womb and will bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel.” What can be said more openly than this? The Jews who killed him used to read these things. If anyone thinks we invent them, let him ask them—let him take them from those enemies especially: testimony for proving the truth is firm enough when it is offered by the enemies themselves.

Yet he was never called Emmanuel, but Jesus, which in Latin means “saving” or “savior,” because he came as salvation-bringer to all the nations; but by this name the prophet declared that God was about to come to humans in flesh. For Emmanuel means “God with us,” namely because, when he was born through the virgin, humans ought to confess that God was with them—that is, on earth and in mortal flesh. Whence David in Psalm 84: “Truth has sprung from the earth,” because God, in whom truth is, received an earthly body, that he might open the way of salvation to the earthly. Isaiah again speaks of the savior sprouting from the earth, and of the boy born whose name is “messenger of great counsel.” For he was sent by God the Father to reveal to all the nations under heaven the holy mystery of the one and true God, taken away from the faithless people who often offended against God.

Daniel also spoke beforehand: “I was watching in a vision of the night: and behold, coming in the clouds of heaven as a son of man…” How then do the Jews both confess and hope for the Christ of God, whom they had rejected because he was born from a human? For God has so arranged that the same Christ come twice to the earth—once that he may announce the one God to the nations, then again that he may reign. The prophet has comprised both comings: “Behold, coming in the clouds of heaven as a son of man.” He did not say “as Son of God,” but “as son of man,” to show that he would put on flesh on earth, teach justice, reveal the truth, be punished with death so as to conquer the underworld, and at last rise and go to the Father, lifted in a cloud. David also: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right…” Even now he has perpetual power as the nations venerate his name; and afterward, when he comes again in clarity and power, he will judge every soul.

latin: Descendens itaque de caelo sanctus ille spiritus dei sanctam uirginem cuius utero se insinuaret elegit. at illa diuino spiritu hausto repleta concepit et sine ullo adtactu uiri repente uirginalis uterus intumuit. quodsi animalia quaedam uento et aura concipere solere omnibus notum est, cur quisquam mirum putet, cum dei spiritu, cui facile est quidquid uelit, grauatam esse uirginem dicimus? quod sane incredibile posset uideri, nisi hoc futurum ante multa saecula prophetae cecinissent. Solomon in ode undeuicesima ita dicit: infirmatus est uterus uirginis et accepit fetum, et grauata est et facta est in multa miseratione mater uirgo. item propheta Esaias, cuius uerba sunt haec: propter hoc dabit deus ipse uobis signum: ecce uirgo accipiet in uterum et pariet filium, et uocabitis nomen eius Emmanuel. quid hoc manifestius dici potest? legebant ista Iudaei qui eum necauerunt. si quis nos haec fingere arbitratur, ab his requirat, ab his potissimum sumat: satis firmum testimonium est ad probandam ueritatem quod ab ipsis perhibetur inimicis. Emmanuel autem numquam uocitatus est, sed Iesus, qui latine dicitur salutaris siue saluator, quia cunctis gentibus salutifer uenit: sed propheta declarauit hoc nomine quod deus ad homines in carne uenturus esset. Emmanuel enim significat \'nobiscum deus\', scilicet quia illo per uirginem nato confiteri homines oportebat deum secum esse id est in terra et in carne mortali. unde Dauid in psalmo LXXXIIII ueritas inquit de terra orta est, quia deus, in quo ueritas est, terrenum corpus accepit, ut terrenis uiam salutis aperiret. item Esaias ipse: ipsi autem non crediderunt et exacerbauerunt spiritum sanctum et conuersus est eis ad inimicitiam. et ipse expugnauit et recordatus est dierum saeculi, qui suscitauit de terra pastorem ouium. quis autem futurus esset ille pastor, declarauit alio loco dicens: exsultent caeli desuper et nubes induant iustitiam, aperiatur terra. et pullulet saluator. ego enim dominus deus creaui eum. saluator uero est, ut supra diximus, Iesus. sed et alio loco idem propheta sic praedicauit: ecce natus est uobis puer, et datus est uobis filius, cuius imperium super umeros eius: et uocatum est nomen eius \'magni consilii nuntius\'. idcirco enim missus est a deo patre, ut uniuersis gentibus quae sub caelo sunt singularis et ueri dei sanctum mysterium reuelaret ablatum perfido populo, qui aduersus deum saepe deliquit. Daniel quoque similia praelocutus est. uidebam inquit in uisu noctis: et ecce in nubibus caeli ut filius hominis ueniens et usque ad uetustum dierum peruenit. et qui adsistebant, obtulerunt eum: et datum est ei regnum et honor et imperium, et omnes populi tribus linguae seruient ei, et potestas eius aeterna, quae numquam transibit et regnum eius non corrumpetur.

quomodo igitur Iudaei et conStentur et sperant Christum dei, qui hunc idcirco reprobauerant, quia ex homine natus est? nam cum ita sit a deo constitutum, ut idem Christus bis adueniat in terram, semel ut unum deum gentibus nuntiet, deinde rursus ut regnet, quomodo in secundum eius aduentum credunt qui in primum non crediderunt? atquin propheta utrosque aduentus eius paucis uerbis comprehendit. ecce inquit in nubibus caeli ut filius hominis ueniens. non dixit ut filius dei, sed ut filius hominis, ut ostenderet quod carne indui haberet in terra, ut suscepta hominis figura et condicione mortali doceret homines iustitiam et cum mandatis dei functus ueritatem gentibus reuelasset, multaretur etiam morte, ut inferos quoque uinceret ac resignaret atque ita demum resurgens ad patrem proficisceretur in nube sublatus. adiecit enim propheta et ait: et usque ad anticum dierum peruenit et oblatus est ei. anticum dierum appellauit deum summum, cuius aetas et origo non potest conprehendi, quia solus a saeculis fuit, ut erit semper in saecula. author: Lactantius
english: Since we have spoken of the second birth, by which he showed himself to humans in flesh, let us come to those wondrous works which, though they were signs of heavenly power, the Jews thought magical. When he first began to grow up, he was dipped by the prophet John in the Jordan river, that by a spiritual washing he might abolish not his own sins—which he assuredly did not have—but those of the flesh he was bearing, so that just as he would save the Jews by the circumcision he undertook, so also he would save the nations by baptism, that is by the pouring of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” which voice is found predicted in David. And the Spirit of God descended upon him, formed in the appearance of a white dove.

From then he began to work the greatest powers—not by magical tricks, which show nothing true and solid, but by heavenly force and power, which had long been sung by the announcing prophets. The works are so many that one book is not enough to cover them all. I will therefore recount them briefly and by kinds, without naming persons and places, so that I may reach the account of his passion and cross. Wherever he went he restored the sick and weak and those laboring under every kind of disease to health in one word and one moment—so that those seized in all their limbs, suddenly strengthened, themselves carried back the beds on which they had a little earlier been brought. To the lame he gave not only walking but even running. He restored to their former sight eyes that had been in deepest darkness. He loosed the tongues of the mute into speech, opened hearing for the deaf, and cleansed those polluted and sprinkled with spots. And he did all this not by hands or some remedy, but by word and command—as the Sibyl also had predicted—nor is it any wonder that he did wonders by a word, when he himself was the Word of God.

He also stilled winds by a word and walked the raging sea; he raised the dead and from one basket there was bread enough for men—as other Sibylline lines also say. Some, leaving these testimonies, usually flee to this: that those songs are not Sibylline but invented and composed by our people. Anyone who has read Cicero and Varro and other ancients who mention the Erythraean Sibyl and the rest will not think that; those authors died before Christ was born according to the flesh. But I do not doubt that those songs were held for delirium in earlier times, when no one understood them: they denounced monstrous miracles whose reason, time, and author were not marked. So they lay through many ages; afterward they were noticed, when the birth of Christ and the passion opened the secrets—just as also the voices of the prophets, which though read by the people of the Jews for a thousand five hundred years and more were not understood until Christ interpreted them by word and works. For the prophets had announced him, and what they spoke could in no way be understood unless the whole had been fulfilled.

author: Lactantius
english: What more can still be said of the Jews’ crime than that they were then blinded and seized by incurable fury—they who, reading these things every day, neither understood them nor could keep themselves from doing them? So, hung upon the cross, he cried out to God with a great voice and of his own will laid down his spirit. At that same hour there was an earthquake, and the temple veil that separated the two tabernacles was torn in two, and the sun was suddenly withdrawn, and from the sixth hour to the ninth there was darkness. Amos the prophet testifies to this: “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at midday, and the day of light shall be darkened; and I will turn your feast days into mourning and your songs into lamentation.” Likewise Jeremiah: “She who gives birth is terrified, and the soul has grown weary, and the sun has gone down for her while it was still midday; she is crushed and cursed; I will give the rest of them to the sword before their enemies.” And the Sibyl: “The curtain of the temple shall be torn, and at midday there shall be a dark, monstrous night for three hours.”

When these things had happened, they could not even understand their crime by the heavenly prodigies. But because he had foretold that he would rise from the underworld on the third day, fearing that if the disciples stole the body everyone would believe he had risen and the confusion among the people would grow far greater, they took him down from the cross, shut him in a tomb, and surrounded it with a firm military guard. Yet on the third day, before light, an earthquake suddenly opened the tomb, and while the guards—stunned with terror—saw nothing, he came out of the tomb whole and alive and went into Galilee to seek his disciples; in the tomb nothing was found except the wrappings in which they had enclosed the wrapped body. The prophets had sung that he would not remain among the dead but would rise on the third day. David in Psalm 15: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you let your holy one see corruption.” Likewise in the third: “I slept and took sleep, and I rose, because the Lord helped me.” Hosea also, first of the twelve prophets, testified to his resurrection: “This is my wise son… and from the hand of the underworld I will deliver him. Where is your judgment, death, or where is your sting?” And elsewhere: “He will make us live after two days, on the third day.” So the Sibyl said he would set a limit to death after a three-day sleep: after finishing death’s portion by sleeping the third day, he would return from the dead into the light, first to show the beginning of resurrection to the called. For by overcoming death he acquired life for us. Therefore no other hope of obtaining immortality is given to a human being unless he believes in him and takes up the cross that must be carried and endured.
